name: Methylsulfonylmethane (MSM)
lead: Methylsulfonylmethane (MSM, dimethyl sulfone) is a small organic sulfur compound, (CH3)2SO2, that occurs naturally in trace amounts in some plants, foods and human blood. It is sold as a dietary supplement for joint comfort, skin, hair and nails, and it appears in topical products. [1][2]

The US FDA has not approved MSM for any medical use, though a manufacturer's 2007 notification that a branded form is generally recognised as safe (GRAS) received a non-objection letter in 2008. [2] Wikipedia describes the evidence for most claims as weak. Small randomised trials of skin and hair outcomes exist, while an osteoarthritis review reported no definitive evidence of superiority over placebo. [2]
On looksmax.org it is discussed for skin, hair texture and joint health, with claims about skin or eye lightening that appear in anecdote only. [3]
infobox: Trace amounts in many foods; found in human blood and CSF [2]
Oral tablets or powder; topical products [3]
GRAS non-objection letter GRN 000229, Feb 2008 (branded form) [2]
About $9-10 for tablets, about $23 for a pound of powder [3]

paras: MSM is a white crystalline solid, soluble in water, and chemically fairly inert. It is formed by oxidation of dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO) and is an intermediate in the oxidation of dimethyl sulfide in the environment. [2] In humans it is thought to come from diet, gut bacteria and endogenous metabolism, and NMR studies have detected it in blood and cerebrospinal fluid. [2]

Supplement makers promote MSM for skin firmness, wrinkles, hair and nails. A 2015 randomised trial in 20 women taking MSM reported fewer and less severe wrinkles and better firmness and texture, a second 20-person study tested two doses and reported improved wrinkles, firmness and hydration, and an Italian RCT of a combination product reported better facial hydration and elasticity. [2] Hair and nail appearance outcomes were reported in the same programme of work. [2]

MSM is widely sold for joint pain. A 2008 systematic review of osteoarthritis trials reported methodological problems and no definitive evidence of benefit over placebo. [2] Small studies have also examined exercise recovery, seasonal allergic rhinitis and immune function. [2]

The skin studies are small (about 20 participants), short, and often involve combination products, so Wikipedia characterises evidence as weak overall. [2] Wikipedia also notes that, in topical products, MSM's potential to enhance skin permeation, like DMSO, must be separated from any direct active effect. [2]

Animal research indicates very low oral and topical toxicity, and the Natural Medicines database rates MSM "possibly safe" at therapeutic doses. [2] A nematode study reported decreased lifespan and fertility at high doses; the relevance to humans is unknown. [2] MSM has also been reported as a cutting agent in illicit methamphetamine. [2]

The sulfur-supplement rationale is credited to biochemist Robert Herschler, who filed a 1982 patent for MSM as a dietary supplement, issued in 1985. [2] Research on DMSO metabolites in 1975 first characterised MSM as a metabolite. [2]

A looksmax.org informational thread describes MSM as a sulfur compound for joints, skin softening and lightening, and hair strength, and the original poster states that the information is largely anecdotal because research on eye or skin colour is sparse. [3] One reply reports no confirmation of those benefits after five years but continued use for joint comfort and spinal height maintenance. [3]

Registered and published human trials have examined MSM for knee osteoarthritis (several trials, including a 100-participant phase 1 study and a completed randomised study), low back pain (phase 3, 100 participants), knee laxity, cardiometabolic health in obesity, allergen-induced nasal symptoms and aromatase-inhibitor joint pain. [4][5][6][7][8][9][10] Published skin and hair trials are small, as above. [2] Results of most registered studies are not summarised in the registry records reviewed.

timeline.event: Kocsis and colleagues publish on DMSO metabolites. [2]
Robert Herschler files a patent for MSM as a dietary supplement (issued 1985). [2]
GRAS notification and FDA non-objection letter for a branded MSM. [2]
Systematic review finds no definitive evidence of benefit in knee osteoarthritis. [2]

lore.intro: Looksmaxxing forums discuss MSM mainly for skin and hair quality and joint health, often with the caveat that evidence is anecdotal. [3]

claims.believers: The thread's author reports detoxifying, softening and lightening effects from anecdotal accounts on skin-care forums. [3]
claims.experts: Small trials report improved wrinkles, firmness and hydration, but none is described as measuring lightening. [2]

claims.claim: MSM can lighten eye colour at high intake
claims.believers: Some posters argue megadosing lightened their eye colour, especially with a light-eyed parent. [3]
claims.experts: No published studies have examined eye colour change from MSM.

claims.claim: MSM improves hair texture and strength
claims.believers: Posters say it improves hair strength and may loosen curls slightly. [3]
claims.experts: One trial programme reported improved hair shine, volume and appearance. [2]

claims.claim: MSM relieves joint pain and helps maintain height through the day
claims.believers: A user reports taking it for years for spinal and joint comfort, and another for ankle and wrist pain. [3]
claims.experts: A 2008 systematic review found no definitive evidence of benefit over placebo in knee osteoarthritis. [2]

card.summary: Sulfur supplement sold for skin, hair and joints; a few small skin trials, with limited evidence overall.
card.note: Eye- and skin-lightening claims come from anecdote only.

quick.overview:
MSM is a sulfur compound found in trace amounts in foods and sold as a supplement for joints, skin, hair and nails. It is cheap and widely available.

Small trials report improved wrinkles and hydration, but they are tiny and short. Claims about lightening skin or eye colour appear only in anecdotes.
quick.mechanism: How MSM acts in the body is poorly understood. It is related to DMSO and may have anti-inflammatory and antioxidant effects in lab studies. In topical products it may help other ingredients penetrate skin.
quick.risks: Animal studies suggest very low toxicity and it has a GRAS non-objection letter for a branded form. It has no approved medical uses. Human long-term data are limited.
